label: g1_ledger
name: Hadamard-E8 lattice KV
mech: Each 128-dimensional head vector is rotated by a seeded random Hadamard transform, which spreads key outlier channels across all dimensions. The query gets the same rotation, so q·k is unchanged and keys can be stored post-RoPE. Keys use an E8 lattice code (2-bit E8P plus 1-bit residual, 3 bits per value). Values use 2-bit E8P. Each token and head also stores one FP8 scale. The first 4 sink tokens and the last 128 tokens stay in FP8. The fused FlashDecoding kernel decodes codewords from a 256-entry table in shared memory. Effective size is about 2.6 bits per value with metadata, or 6.1× smaller than FP16. On MLA models, the decoupled 64-dim RoPE part stays in FP8. The closest earlier attempt is VecInfer/MILLION, which used learned codebooks at a uniform 2 bits and broke long-CoT output. This design spends the extra bit on keys and uses a lattice code that needs no data. The deciding quantity is the AIME accuracy change at 32k tokens.
value: It cuts decode KV reads about 6× (about 1.7× cheaper per token in Archetype B), with predicted loss of ≤1% on RULER-64k and LongBench and ≤2 points on AIME24. It is falsified if R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on AIME24 loses more than 2 points versus FP16, a test of about 2 GPU-hours.

label: g1_ledger
name: Progressive bit-plane attention
mech: K and V are stored after a Hadamard rotation as a 2-bit base plane plus a 2-bit refinement plane, with per-group FP8 scales, for about 4.3 bits per value in total. On each decode step the kernel first scores all tokens using the base plane. It then reads refinement planes only for the top 2% of pages by score plus the sink pages, and recomputes their logits and values at 4-bit precision. The closest earlier attempts are Quest and ShadowKV, which skip pages entirely and therefore act like eviction. Here every token is still attended, and only precision varies with the query, so multi-turn reuse and question changes are safe. The deciding quantity is the attention mass covered by the top 2%, which must be at least 99% on long CoT.
value: HBM reads fall to about 2.2 bits per value (about 7× fewer than FP16) at roughly NVFP4 quality. Refinement planes can be offloaded to host memory to gain capacity. The added cost is an estimated 10–15% from the two-pass kernel. It is falsified if logit KL divergence versus FP16 exceeds NVFP4's on RULER-niah-multikey.

label: g1_ledger
name: Entropy-coded rotated tier cache
mech: For the CPU/SSD prefix tier (LMCache or HiCache), K and V are Hadamard-rotated, quantized with a uniform step at 5-bit-equivalent mean squared error, and rANS-coded per page. Entropy-constrained scalar quantization saves about 0.5 bits over Lloyd-Max at equal error on Gaussian-like rotated data, so pages land near 3.5 bits per value plus a 1% table cost. The GPU decodes pages to FP8 on load. The closest earlier attempt is SplitZip, which only coded BF16 exponents and reached about 1.33×. This design codes after rotation and quantization, where the entropy gap is large. The deciding quantity is GPU rANS decode throughput, which must exceed about 50 GB/s of output so it stays below PCIe and NVMe bandwidth.
value: Each tier byte holds about 2.3× more prefixes than an FP8 tier at better-than-NVFP4 fidelity, which raises the multi-turn hit rate. It is falsified if the measured entropy of rotated KV codes on Llama-3-70B is above 4 bits per value.

label: g1_neg
name: Bit-plane on-demand attention precision
mech: Keys are stored pre-RoPE and rotated, then quantized to 4-bit codes laid out as bit-planes, at 4.5 bits per value in HBM. A FlashAttention tile reads only the top 2 planes plus scales (2.5 bits per value, 6.4× fewer bytes than FP16) to score every token. It then fetches the low planes only for the ≈2% of tokens whose coarse logit could land in the top softmax mass; the 4 sink tokens and a 64-token recent window always use full planes. The closest earlier attempts are Quest and ShadowKV, which drop the tokens they do not select and so lose them on reused or multi-turn queries; here no token is ever dropped, and the tail is still read at 2 bits. The deciding quantity is the softmax mass that falls on coarse-only tokens multiplied by their value error; it must stay ≤1e-3 per head.
value: About 2.6 bits read per value during decode, against NVFP4's 4.5. This should give a 1.5–1.6× decode speedup in reasoning workloads, with quality bounded by NVFP4 (≤1% drop on AIME24 and RULER-64K for R1-Distill-8B). It is falsified if a one-day PyTorch prototype misses NVFP4 accuracy on AIME24.

label: g1_neg
name: Cross-layer conditional entropy coding
mech: Values and pre-RoPE keys are rotated and quantized to NVFP4-grade 4-bit codes. Each token's codes at layer l are then coded losslessly with interleaved rANS, using a small count table conditioned on the same channel's code at layer l−1 and at token t−1. Pages decompress into SRAM inside the attention kernel or on transfer from a CPU or SSD tier. The closest earlier attempts are SplitZip and ZipNN, which code only BF16 exponents and reach about 25%; here the target is low-entropy indices that share the residual stream across layers. The deciding quantity is the conditional entropy H(code_l | code_{l−1}, code_{t−1}), which must be ≤2.5 bits.
value: Output is bit-identical to the 4-bit format, at ≈3.0 bits per value including tables and scales, or 5.3× vs FP16. This raises prefix-cache hit rates and the number of resident requests in LMCache-style deployments. GPU rANS throughput of roughly 300 GB/s (DietGPU class) limits its speed advantage in decode-heavy HBM serving. Measuring that entropy on 1k cached sequences from Llama-3-70B and DeepSeek-V3 latents falsifies it in one hour.

label: g1_neg
name: Calibration-free trellis-coded KV
mech: Each rotated 256-value token-channel block is coded with a QTIP-style trellis code over a fixed Gaussian code. This is sequence-level vector quantization at 2 bits plus one FP8 scale per 64 values, 2.13 bits per value or 7.5× vs FP16. A lookup-free decode fuses into the attention tile. The closest earlier attempts are KIVI-2bit and VecInfer, whose scalar or small-codebook error collapses long chains of thought; trellis codes cut MSE about 2× over scalar quantization at equal bits.
value: The deciding quantity is attention-logit MSE relative to 4-bit scalar codes, which must be ≤1.2×. If that holds, the target is ≤1% relative drop on AIME24, GSM8K, RULER-128K and NIAH for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3-70B at 7.5×, with ≈10% decode overhead. A 2-hour logit-MSE sweep falsifies it.

label: g1_mech
name: Asymmetric dithered key-value codes
mech: Keys are rotated before RoPE and stored at 3 bits per channel group, plus one FP16 scale per 128 values, which is 3.125 bits. Values are stored at 2 bits per token group with dither subtracted from a shared seed, so the dither needs no stored metadata. That is 2.125 bits, for an average of about 2.65 bits, or 6.0× vs FP16. The reasoning is that score error is exponentiated, while value error averages out over the attended tokens. The closest earlier attempt is KIVI K2V2, which lost 13 points on AIME. Its 2-bit keys broke sharp attention and its error was deterministic and biased; this design keeps keys at 3 bits and makes value error unbiased. The deciding quantity is the effective number of attended tokens in retrieval heads. If it is below about 4, the value noise does not average out.
value: 6× KV capacity with projected loss of ≤1% on RULER-64k and GSM8K and ≤2 points on AIME, and no calibration.

label: g1_mech
name: Bound-driven progressive bit-plane reads
mech: Rotated keys and values are stored as 6-bit codes split into bit-planes. The top 2 planes plus scales, about 2.2 bits, stay in HBM, which is 7.3×. The lower 4 planes go to CPU memory. On each decode step the kernel computes an interval for every token's score from the coarse planes. It fetches finer planes only for tokens whose upper bound could carry more than ε=10⁻³ of the attention mass, so the error is provably bounded. The closest earlier attempts are Quest and ShadowKV, which use approximate page-level selection and skip tokens. This design never skips a token; it refines precision. The deciding quantity is the fraction of tokens refined per step. It must stay below about 2% at 128k to fit in PCIe bandwidth.
value: 7× HBM savings with a guaranteed attention-error bound, which makes it safe for chains of thought and reuse.

label: g1_mech
name: Entropy-measured per-head bit allocation
mech: During prefill, compute each KV head's attention entropy over the prompt's own queries. Assign bit widths from that: broad heads get K2V1, middle heads K3V2, and sharp retrieval heads K4V4. Every token is kept, and the bits average about 2.1 including scales, or 7.5×. The closest earlier attempts are RazorAttention and DuoAttention. They evicted tokens in non-retrieval heads and saved only 1.67× on GQA. This design only lowers precision, which works on already-shared GQA heads and keeps multi-turn reuse safe. The deciding quantity is how stable head entropy rankings are across prompts and decode phases, measured by a Spearman rank correlation of at least 0.9.
value: About 7.5× compression without calibration data, adapting per prompt to any GQA model.

label: g1_rf1
name: Margin-flagged key residual promotion
mech: Each head is rotated with a fixed Hadamard transform, which needs no calibration. Keys are stored at 2 bits pre-RoPE, values at 2 bits per token, and a 2-bit residual for every page is kept in host memory. During decode, the kernel flags any page whose quantized logit lies within ‖q‖·‖e‖max of the top logit. Only flagged pages fetch their residual over PCIe, so they are read at 4 bits. The closest earlier attempt is Kitty's dynamic precision boost, which uses a static importance heuristic and still trails FP16 by 3–4 AIME points. This design promotes exactly the pairs whose argmax can flip. The deciding quantity is the flagged-page fraction, which must stay under about 5% to fit PCIe bandwidth.
value: About 2.3 bits per value in HBM (7× vs FP16) with 4-bit fidelity where reasoning needs it, so batch size roughly doubles over NVFP4.

label: g1_rf1
name: Entropy-gated decision-step recompute
mech: Decode runs on a 2.3-bit rotated cache. A full FP8 copy is kept on host or SSD, as LMCache already does. When next-token entropy exceeds a threshold τ, the step is a decision point. The model then refetches FP8 pages for the top-attention pages identified in the quantized pass, recomputes that step, and samples from the corrected distribution. The closest earlier attempt is speculative-decoding verification, which rechecks every token at full cost. This design rechecks only uncertain steps, and only on pages that carry attention mass. The deciding quantity is the fraction of steps above τ, which must be under about 10% for the overhead to stay below 15%.
value: It bounds where a 7× cache can change a reasoning chain's tokens, without any offline calibration.

label: g1_rf1
name: Per-request online KLT bit-allocation
mech: During prefill, the system accumulates each head's pre-RoPE key and value covariance. It stores one 128×128 FP16 basis per head per layer, which is under 0.01 bits per value at 32k. Bits are then allocated by reverse water-filling, about 2.5 on average, and RoPE is applied after dequantization inside the kernel. The closest earlier attempt is Palu, whose offline SVD truncation creates latent outliers and loses accuracy beyond 30% rank reduction. This design truncates nothing and needs no calibration data. The deciding quantity is the eigenvalue arithmetic-to-geometric-mean ratio, which must be at least 4 to save at least 1 bit. That ratio is likely too small on MLA latents.
value: For GQA models it is a calibration-free path to 2.5 bits per value (6.4×) whose quality follows rate-distortion theory rather than heuristics.

label: g1_rf2
name: Hadamard-trellis 2-bit KV
mech: Each pre-RoPE key and value head vector is rotated by a fixed random Hadamard matrix and stored as one FP16 norm plus trellis-coded indices at 1.875 bits per value. Four sink tokens and the last 128 tokens stay in FP8. The fused decode kernel decodes the trellis in registers, then applies RoPE and runs attention. The closest earlier attempt is TurboQuant, which lost 18 GSM8K points at 3 bits because its scalar bins plus noisy QJL correction waste about 3 dB. Trellis vector coding recovers about 2 dB of that, and the design has no QJL stage. The deciding quantity is the logit error relative to the per-head logit spread.
value: A drop-in, calibration-free 8× KV cache versus FP16, about 2× smaller than NVFP4, which should give roughly 1.6–2× reasoning decode throughput.

label: g1_rf2
name: Coarse-HBM, refined-host residual
mech: The HBM holds only 2-bit rotated codes, and every token is still attended. A 2-bit residual for each token sits in host DRAM. At each decode step, approximate scores from the 2-bit codes pick the top 256 tokens per KV head, and only those tokens' residuals are fetched. That costs about 10 MB per step for a 70B model at 128k, roughly 0.2 ms over PCIe 5 or less over NVLink-C2C. The closest earlier attempts are Quest and ShadowKV, which approximate or skip non-selected tokens. Here no token is dropped, so multi-turn reuse is safe. The deciding quantity is the softmax mass that falls outside the top-k set.
value: About 4-bit effective fidelity on the tokens that matter, at a 2-bit HBM footprint and read cost.

label: g1_rf2
name: MLA latent trellis quantization
mech: The 512-dimension MLA latent is Hadamard-rotated and trellis-coded at 2 bits. The decoupled 64-dimension RoPE key stays in FP8, and one FP16 norm is stored per token. That totals about 2.7 bits per value, roughly 6× smaller than the BF16 MLA cache. The kernel decodes the latent before the absorbed up-projection. The closest earlier attempt is Palu, whose own low-rank projection created latent outliers that hurt low-bit quantization. Rotation flattens those outliers without calibration. The deciding quantity is the latent MSE after the absorbed up-projection.
value: Removes about 25% of DeepSeek-V3-class decode cost and fits about 6× more 128k contexts per GPU.

label: repair
name: RoPE-band-ranked Hadamard-E8 KV
mech: Anchor kept: a seeded Hadamard rotation plus an E8 lattice code decoded from a 256-entry shared-memory table. The original design rotated all 128 dimensions globally at one rate, and that is now published work (arXiv 2610.15384, E8 k2v2). It is also the configuration that collapses on reasoning: TurboQuant-MSE K3V2, which uses one rotation and one rate, scores 0.0 on AIME24 (Block-GTQ paper). In the repaired design, the 64 RoPE pairs are ranked by their prefill energy. RoPE never changes a pair's norm, so the ranking holds during decode. They are grouped into 16 bands of 8 dimensions, with a Hadamard rotation inside each band. Bands are coded at 4, 3 or 2 bits with E8 (2b+2b residual, 2b+1b, 2b), giving keys a 3.0-bit average. Values use E8 at 2 bits, which is where E8 helps most. Simulated MSE is 0.091 for E8 against 0.118 for Lloyd-Max and 0.25 for KIVI-style INT2 g128. Each token and head stores one FP8 scale. 4 sink tokens and the last 128 tokens stay in FP16. The query gets the same permutation and band rotation, so keys are stored post-RoPE exactly. Total is 2.62 b/value at 32k (6.1× vs FP16) and 3.0 b at 4k (5.3×). Decode dequantization is 12.5 op/B, under the H100 CUDA-core ridge of about 20 op/B. Prefill encode cost is +0.007%.
value: Same 6× memory and about 6.2× the decode throughput of BF16 at 32k as Block-GTQ K3V2. The prediction is that it loses less on AIME (≤2 points vs −2.5). That would be about $5.06 vs $5.17 per 1,000 correct AIME answers, roughly 2% cheaper, which is a small edge.

label: repair
name: Folded online KLT water-filling
mech: Anchor kept: each request accumulates its own covariance during prefill, takes a KLT basis from it, and allocates bits per component by reverse water-filling, with no calibration data. The fatal step was rebuilding every key (819 FLOP/B against a 295 FLOP/B ridge). That is removed by computing the KLT on post-RoPE keys, so attention scores from the stored coefficients using q′ = Uᵀq, and by folding the value basis into the output (o = U_v·Σp·c). This adds +0.39% decode FLOPs at 32k. The distortion is weighted by the request's own prefill query covariance. The basis is refreshed every 32k generated tokens. Prompts under 1,024 tokens fall back to Hadamard. The corrected basis overhead is 0.0625 b/value per FP16 basis at 32k, not "<0.01". Total is about 2.74 b at 32k (5.8×). The model's decisive number is that the post-RoPE KLT gains only 0.0–0.3 b over plain RoPE-band energy allocation on RoPE keys. On stores with no RoPE it gains 0.17–1.6 b over Hadamard: values, MLA latents c_KV (folded into the absorbed W_UK/W_UV) and NoPE layers. So the design is retargeted at those stores.
value: For MLA models (DeepSeek-V3/R1, Kimi-K2) and NoPE/iRoPE layers, it is a calibration-free way to read a compressed cache directly in HBM. If the real-tensor gain is ≥0.5 b, it would be about 1.2× cheaper per served token than Hadamard/TurboQuant at the same quality. On ordinary RoPE keys it is about equal to Block-GTQ (≈1.0×).

label: repair
name: Mass-gated dithered value codes
mech: The anchor stays: keys and values are treated differently. Keys are always deterministic 4-bit (per-channel, 128-token groups, 4.25 bits with scales), because key error is exponentiated in the softmax. Values carry a subtractive dither regenerated from a position hash, so it costs no stored bits. The repair is where the dither matters. It does not reduce error per value (0.50 relative RMS at 2 bits either way), and simple per-block mean-centering beats it on channel-offset data (0.49 vs 1.33). It is, however, the only one of the three schemes that makes errors on repeated content (repeated phrases, code, CoT loops) shrink as more tokens are averaged: at 60 copies, 0.065 vs 0.44–0.52 for the other schemes. That makes a provable gate possible. Each KV head's value precision is chosen from E_h = √Σp² over its quantized tokens: 4-bit above 0.31, 3-bit for 0.133–0.31, 2-bit for 0.046–0.133, and 1-bit dithered at or below 0.046 (about 470 or more tokens effectively attended). At that 1-bit setting the simulated error is 0.025–0.063, under the 0.10 that single-token 4-bit already gives, while deterministic 1-bit stays at 0.38–1.10. Values are Hadamard-rotated and mean-centered, 4 sink tokens plus the last 128 tokens stay FP16, and E_h is accumulated inside the attention kernel (the maximum over the GQA group, 99th percentile over queries).
value: 3.46–3.95 bits (4.1–4.6×), with total attention-output error at most 1.2–1.43× that of uniform 4-bit. That is 55–60 vs 50 concurrent 32k requests on an H100 (+10–20% requests per GPU), with no calibration.

label: repair
name: Window-mass per-head precision gating
mech: The anchor stays: each KV head's precision is set per prompt from the prompt's own attention, measured during prefill, and no token is dropped. Four repairs remove the causes of death. First, 1-bit and 2-bit keys are banned; the menu is now K4V4, K4V3 or K3V2. Second, there is an error target instead of a fixed 2.1-bit budget. Third, ranking heads by entropy (which needed Spearman stability across prompts) is replaced by an absolute gate on m_q, the share of attention that falls outside the FP16 sink-plus-recent window. Fourth, every head gets per-block channel-mean centering (0.125 bit). Deterministic error can stay correlated across tokens, but it is still bounded by rel(b)·m_q, so the gate holds without dither. The thresholds are K3V2 if m_q ≤ 0.133, K4V3 if m_q ≤ 0.31, and K4V4 otherwise. A decode-time Σp² watchdog upgrades a head's new 128-token blocks if it turns sharp during chain-of-thought.
value: 3.22–3.80 bits (4.2–5.0×), with error at most 1.2–1.67× that of uniform 4-bit. That is 57–67 vs 50 concurrent requests (+14–34%). It matches the calibrated KVTuner (about 3.5 bits) while needing no calibration, and it beats uniform K3V3 (3.31 bits, about 2.15× error) on error at the same size.
